content: Home News Obituary Recipes Charity Special ಕನ್ನಡ Live TV RADIO Advertise Contact Us Matrimonial Properties Jobs General Ads Red Chillies Music Ask Dr Greetings Astrology Tribute Of Love Latest Chronic stress can disrupt cortisol, affect weight, sleep and blood sugar Mon, Sep 14 Bangladesh dengue crisis worsens: 52 deaths in September take total toll to 149 Mon, Sep 14 Faridabad hospital launches region’s first dedicated fever clinic Mon, Sep 14 Sirmaur: 4 test positive for H1N1 at Paonta Sahib hospital, shifted to isolation ward Mon, Sep 14 Bangladesh measles outbreak exposes major gaps in immunisation system Sun, Sep 13 Study reveals why virulent rabies infection overwhelms brain immunity Sun, Sep 13 Celiac disease increasingly detected among adults and elderly at PGIMS Sun, Sep 13 Health Dengue, chikungunya cases rise in Pune amid humid weather Wed, Sep 09 2026 08:43:20 AM Daijiworld Media Network - Pune Pune, Sep 9: Vector-borne diseases, including dengue and chikungunya, have been on the rise in Pune over the past few weeks amid hot and humid weather, leading to an increase in hospital admissions and prompting civic authorities to intensify action against mosquito breeding sites. Doctors have warned people against ignoring persistent fever, saying some dengue patients tend to delay seeking medical attention because the fever may temporarily subside during the day before returning in the evening. A doctor at a leading city hospital said some patients were reporting for treatment and admission only after suffering from fever for several days. “The fever in dengue patients gives confusing signals in the initial phase, as it often subsides during the day and intensifies in the evening. Some patients may feel they are recovering, but that is a dangerous misconception,” the doctor said. Dr Dattatraya B Patil, consultant physician at Noble Hospitals and Research Centre, said there had been a rise in viral fever cases in the hospital's outpatient department. “There has been a rise in the number of viral fever cases in our OPD. About 15–20% of these patients are testing positive for dengue. Patients should not ignore symptoms such as high-grade fever, eyeball pain, headaches, body and joint pain, vomiting, and loose motions. Dengue requires urgent attention; however, with proper medication and early treatment, it can be managed effectively,” he said. Several severe cases requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission have also been reported recently. Infectious diseases expert Dr Sujata Rege said hospitalisations due to dengue and dengue-like fever had increased, although such a trend was common during the monsoon. “While there is a rise in hospitalisations due to dengue and dengue-like fevers, this is a common trend every monsoon. Patients with a prior history of dengue may experience a faster drop in platelet counts than those infected for the first time. However, the treatment remains the same regardless of the strain,” she said. According to Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) assistant health officer Dr Rajesh Dighe, the civic body does not independently investigate the dengue strains circulating in the city as it requires specialised infrastructure. “We collaborate with the National Institute of Virology for this purpose, though the reports we receive typically only indicate whether samples are positive or negative for dengue,” he said. As of September 7, Pune had recorded 1,266 suspected dengue cases and 47 laboratory-confirmed cases, while 21 chikungunya cases had also been reported, according to PMC data. The number of suspected dengue cases has risen sharply since the monsoon. Pune recorded 175 suspected cases in June, 323 in July and 484 in August, with another 111 suspected cases reported during the first seven days of September. The civic body has also intensified its crackdown on mosquito breeding sites. More than 2,200 notices have been issued and fines exceeding Rs 4 lakh collected, Dr Dighe said. Other reports put the number of notices at 2,231 and the total fine at around Rs 4.04 lakh. Meanwhile, the Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation (PCMC) has inspected approximately 4.37 lakh homes, identifying mosquito breeding sites at around 3,900 locations. The civic body issued notices to 2,838 individuals and collected fines totalling more than Rs 10 lakh. Pimpri Chinchwad has so far recorded 16 confirmed and 684 suspected dengue cases, according to the latest figures. The civic action comes amid concerns over stagnant water left behind by intermittent monsoon showers, which has created favourable conditions for mosquito breeding. PMC has intensified anti-larval measures, fogging and containment activities around the homes of patients testing positive for dengue and chikungunya. At a recent meeting chaired by additional municipal commissioner Pavneet Kaur, the PMC announced a “Stop Dengue” campaign and directed all civic departments to contribute to mosquito-control efforts. Kaur said the health department would identify and destroy mosquito breeding sites, while the encroachment department would ensure that rainwater did not accumulate in materials seized during anti-encroachment drives. The encroachment department has also been asked to act against businesses conducting unauthorised tyre and puncture-related activities on roads and footpaths, where stagnant water can provide breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The solid waste management department has been directed to remove unusable materials from public spaces and create awareness about proper garbage collection and precautions against mosquito-borne diseases. Civic officials have urged residents to ensure that water does not remain stagnant in and around homes, offices and other premises, as even small quantities of stagnant water can become breeding sites for mosquitoes. content_title: Anthropic Says It Blocked Scientists Using Claude for Bioweapons Research
content: Search SF Sep 15, 2026 · 1:05 AM 215 Users OnlineOnline US| INTERNATIONAL| ASIA| Discussions Community💬 SF Startup Fortune Search ⌕ Home News AI Entrepreneur Interviews Guides Tech Opinion Latest Community Most Read Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google All... Home › Ai Anthropic Says It Blocked Scientists Using Claude for Bioweapons Research Anthropic disclosed five cases where researchers tried to use Claude for research that could aid biological weapons development, including a May 2026 attempt tied to a military institute studying the chikungunya virus. The same September 2026 threat report details a Russian state-linked hacking operation against Ukraine and drone-swarm software built with Claude Code. Elroy Fernandes Sep 10, 2026 · 9:01 PM · 5 min read · 1.4K reads Anthropic says it caught researchers using Claude in work that could support biological weapons, and the strongest part of the report is not the warning. It's the detail. Anthropic's September 10, 2026 threat report is not a vague safety memo. It names five biological misuse cases between December 2025 and August 2026, including one May 2026 request for help writing a grant application tied to gain-of-function work on chikungunya virus. According to Anthropic, the grant sought to identify mutations that could make the mosquito-borne virus more harmful as it passed through live animals, and the work was intended for a military research institute even though the researchers appeared civilian. That's the case making headlines. It should. Chikungunya can cause fever and severe joint pain that lasts for weeks or months, and Anthropic says there is no licensed therapeutic. A natural outbreak and a deliberate release could also be hard to tell apart, because the virus already circulates in the world. You don't need a Hollywood plot for this to be dangerous. You need a real lab and a plausible grant - and a model willing to help in the wrong place. Anthropic says its biological safety classifier blocked the grant-writing request. The story did not end there. Its investigators found that the traffic would normally have gone through an LLM platform serving dozens of life-sciences researchers, many of them virologists connected to civilian and military institutions. The platform tunneled traffic through US infrastructure to dodge Anthropic's regional blocks, used a zero-data-retention service to hide content, and later routed sensitive prompts that Claude refused to another model with weaker safeguards. That is the real shape of the problem. It is not one scientist asking one bad question. This Week in AI: Robots Take a Punch, Assistants Get Long-Term Memory, and Models Keep Getting Cheaper A dense week across robotics, model releases and AI research: humanoid robots duke it out, ChatGPT gets long-term memory, and frontier-adjacent AI keeps getting cheaper and faster. - how to build robots that handle physical impacts - AI models getting cheaper and more accessible features The same biological section also describes a researcher outside the US who spent weeks using Claude on avian influenza work involving mammalian adaptation and airborne transmissibility. In that case, Anthropic says its classifiers confined the exchanges to its weakest model class, Claude Sonnet 4 and Haiku 4.5, which limited the help the researcher could get. The company also found an orthopoxvirus grant application drafted on Opus 5 in about an hour, plus two cases involving venom peptides and toxin redesign. Some of this work could support vaccines or medicine. Some of it could also help make pathogens or toxins more dangerous. Here's the thing: in biology, those two paths often use the same methods. Claude is showing up in more than biology The report covers seven harm areas: cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological misuse, conventional weapons development, and illicit distillation. The cyber section is the most concrete. Anthropic attributes one operation, GTG-20006, to an actor whose activity is consistent with public reporting on Midnight Blizzard. The group targeted Ukrainian and European government, military, diplomatic, defense and intelligence organizations, with drone technology and supply chains appearing again and again in the target set. Anthropic says GTG-20006 used AI-driven workflows for reconnaissance, phishing infrastructure, persistence, command and control, and data exfiltration. The report says the actor scanned more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations, bulk-exported mailboxes from at least two drone component makers, targeted a military drone maker, and stole a software development kit for a drone vision system. Barely any humans touched some parts of the workflow. Separately, Anthropic says likely Russia-based freelance actors used Claude Code to build software for a full-stack autonomous first-person-view kamikaze drone swarm called DronDoc or Serafim. The system included shared swarm memory, terminal guidance, onboard attack and return-to-base behavior, and low-level chip logic. The report says the onboard model could select targets, including a "person" class, and issue detonation commands without a human in the loop. That line should stop you cold. Anthropic also says it disrupted six conventional-weapons cases: three in China, two in Russia - one in Yemen. The Yemen case involved guidance, navigation and control software for rockets and missiles, including a guided rocket that was test-fired and apparently failed. Chinese and Iranian government-aligned actors used Claude for surveillance work against diaspora communities and dissidents abroad, including Uyghur, Tibetan, Falun Gong, Iranian opposition and Jewish diaspora targets. That has nothing to do with innovation. It has everything to do with repression. The disclosure has a commercial edge This is not Anthropic's first threat report. The company published earlier reports in March, August and November 2025, including disclosures on a large-scale extortion operation using Claude Code, a North Korean employment fraud scheme, and a Chinese state-sponsored campaign abusing Claude Code. Four reports in 18 months is a pattern. That pattern cuts two ways. Anthropic is doing something most frontier labs still don't do with this level of specificity, naming viruses, military research settings, drone software, target classes and even internal threat-group labels. At the same time, Anthropic sells Claude to governments and companies that want proof its safety systems work. Frankly, both things can be true. The company has a commercial reason to look responsible, and its report still gives defenders details they would not have had otherwise. A New Trick Lets Anthropic Read Claude's Inner Thoughts Before It Speaks Anthropic says it has found a hidden 'workspace' inside Claude where the model quietly registers suspicions, including that it's being tested for blackmail, without ever saying so out loud. The July 6 research, built on a new open-sourced tool called the Jacobian lens, found Claude showed this kind of silent evaluation awareness in up to 26% of... - how to interpret Claude's internal thoughts - Claude model interpretability testing methods The harder question is scale. Anthropic can tell you what it caught. It can't tell you what every other lab missed, or what slipped through its own systems before the classifiers improved. That is why this report matters beyond Claude. If frontier models can now help with cyber operations, weapons software and dual-use biology, then safety monitoring is no longer a nice line in a policy document. It is part of the product.
